title: Discussion: surfacing Pydantic `json_schema_extra={"readOnly": True}` through to JSON Schema `readOnly` state: OPEN author: candleindark (Isaac To) labels: comments: 0 assignees: projects: milestone: number: 68 -- ## Summary `pydantic2linkml` emits LinkML schemas that downstream tooling (notably [`linkml`'s `JsonSchemaGenerator`][jsg]) translates to JSON Schema. JSON Schema has a well-defined [`readOnly`][js-readonly] keyword, but there is currently no documented or supported way — via this project or via LinkML upstream — to author a slot in the generated LinkML such that it produces `readOnly: true` in the downstream JSON Schema. The concrete motivating case is Pydantic models that already mark fields as read-only via [`Field(..., json_schema_extra={"readOnly": True})`][pyd-jse]. For example, [`dandischema.models`][dandi-models] uses this on `id` and `schemaKey` fields across `DandiBaseModel` and its subclasses. When those models are run through `pydantic2linkml`, the `readOnly` intent is lost: it does not appear in the generated LinkML, and therefore cannot appear in any JSON Schema generated from that LinkML. This issue is a **discussion** issue: it lays out the analysis and the options available today, so we can decide whether `pydantic2linkml` needs to do anything (and if so, what) once the LinkML upstream discussion settles. No concrete code change is proposed here. [jsg]: https://linkml.io/linkml/generators/json-schema.html [js-readonly]: https://json-schema.org/draft/2019-09/json-schema-validation#rfc.section.9.4 [pyd-jse]: https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/api/fields/#pydantic.fields.Field [dandi-models]: https://github.com/dandi/dandischema/blob/master/dandischema/models.py ## Background: `readonly` (LinkML) vs `readOnly` (JSON Schema) LinkML and JSON Schema both have a notion of "read-only," but they are not wired together. - **[JSON Schema `readOnly`][js-readonly]** is defined in the validation/meta-data vocabulary (introduced in draft-07, carried forward unchanged into 2019-09 and 2020-12). It is a boolean annotation indicating that the instance value is managed by the owning authority and should not be modified by consumers. It does not affect validation. In 2019-09 it lives in the meta-data vocabulary (`https://json-schema.org/draft/2019-09/vocab/meta-data`), which is part of the default 2019-09 dialect — i.e., it is available in the JSON Schema dialect that LinkML's generator targets. - **[LinkML `readonly`][lk-readonly]** is defined in the LinkML metamodel as a free-text string: "If present, slot is read only. Text explains why." Operationally it is "truthy string = read-only, with an explanatory reason." [lk-readonly]: https://linkml.io/linkml-model/latest/docs/readonly/ **Neither keyword affects validation behavior** (verified — see "Validation behavior" below). Both are pure annotations: they convey intent to consumers but do not cause a validator to accept or reject any instance. The operational semantics overlap closely: both say "this field exists on the instance but should not be written by clients." The differences are: - LinkML's value is a reason string; JSON Schema's is a boolean. - JSON Schema `readOnly` is a fairly specific client/server contract (heavily used by OpenAPI, often paired with `writeOnly`). LinkML's `readonly` docstring is vaguer, and in practice may be used for "computed/derived," "immutable after creation," or "managed by the system." The stock LinkML `JsonSchemaGenerator` does **not** emit `readOnly` from a slot's `readonly` value. There is no built-in mapping. ## Validation behavior (verified) Both keywords are pure annotations — neither alters whether an instance passes validation. Verified empirically against the relevant validators: ### JSON Schema 2019-09 (`jsonschema` 4.26.0)
check_jsonschema.py ```python """Verify whether JSON Schema `readOnly` affects validation.""" import json import jsonschema schema = { "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2019-09/schema", "type": "object", "properties": { "id": {"type": "string", "readOnly": True}, "name": {"type": "string"}, }, "required": ["id", "name"], } instances = [ {"id": "abc", "name": "alice"}, {"id": "xyz", "name": "bob"}, ] print("=== JSON Schema 2019-09, readOnly: true on `id` ===") for inst in instances: try: jsonschema.validate( inst, schema, cls=jsonschema.Draft201909Validator ) print(f" VALID: {inst}") except jsonschema.ValidationError as e: print(f" INVALID: {inst} -> {e.message}") # Try a wrong-typed value to confirm validation works at all. print("\n=== Sanity: type violation should still fail ===") bad = {"id": 123, "name": "alice"} try: jsonschema.validate(bad, schema, cls=jsonschema.Draft201909Validator) print(f" VALID: {bad}") except jsonschema.ValidationError as e: print(f" INVALID: {bad} -> {e.message}") ```
Output ``` === JSON Schema 2019-09, readOnly: true on `id` === VALID: {'id': 'abc', 'name': 'alice'} VALID: {'id': 'xyz', 'name': 'bob'} === Sanity: type violation should still fail === INVALID: {'id': 123, 'name': 'alice'} -> 123 is not of type 'string' ```
Instances that set the `readOnly` field validate fine; the validator is working (the type-violation sanity check fails as expected). ### LinkML (`linkml` 1.10.0)
schema_readonly.yaml ```yaml id: https://example.org/readonly-test name: readonly_test prefixes: linkml: https://w3id.org/linkml/ imports: - linkml:types default_range: string classes: Thing: attributes: id: identifier: true range: string readonly: "managed by the server; clients must not set this" name: range: string required: true ```
check_linkml.py ```python """Verify whether LinkML `readonly` affects validation.""" from linkml.validator import validate import os SCHEMA = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), "schema_readonly.yaml") instances = [ {"id": "abc", "name": "alice"}, {"id": "xyz", "name": "bob"}, ] print("=== LinkML schema, readonly set on `id` slot ===") for inst in instances: report = validate(inst, schema=SCHEMA, target_class="Thing") if report.results: print(f" INVALID: {inst}") for r in report.results: print(f" - [{r.severity}] {r.message}") else: print(f" VALID: {inst}") # Sanity: a type violation should still fail. print("\n=== Sanity: missing required `name` should still fail ===") bad = {"id": "abc"} report = validate(bad, schema=SCHEMA, target_class="Thing") if report.results: print(f" INVALID: {bad}") for r in report.results: print(f" - [{r.severity}] {r.message}") else: print(f" VALID: {bad}") ```
Output ``` === LinkML schema, readonly set on `id` slot === VALID: {'id': 'abc', 'name': 'alice'} VALID: {'id': 'xyz', 'name': 'bob'} === Sanity: missing required `name` should still fail === INVALID: {'id': 'abc'} - [ERROR] 'name' is a required property in / ```
Instances that set the `readonly`-marked slot validate fine; the validator is working (the missing-required sanity check fails as expected). This strengthens the case that translating LinkML `readonly` to JSON Schema `readOnly` is semantically safe: since neither side enforces anything, no instance that previously validated can be rejected by adding the mapping. ## The case for a LinkML upstream change A reasonable argument: emitting `readOnly: true` whenever a slot has a non-empty `readonly` value preserves the operational semantics, and the explanatory text — which has no JSON Schema equivalent — could optionally be preserved as an annotation (e.g., `x-readonly-reason`). The translation would be defensible and useful as a default, even though it is an interpretation rather than an identity mapping. A companion issue will be filed on `linkml/linkml` proposing this. ## What can a user do today, without upstream changes? Three options exist; none are built into `pydantic2linkml`: 1. **Post-process / overlay the downstream JSON Schema.** Run LinkML → JSON Schema, then deep-merge a small overlay that adds `"readOnly": true` to the relevant property paths. Lowest friction, keeps the LinkML schema clean. Analogous to the `-M` / `-O` overlay/deep-merge flow this project already provides for its LinkML output, but applied one step downstream against the JSON Schema. 2. **Subclass `JsonSchemaGenerator`.** Override the per-slot emission to inspect either the slot's `readonly` value or a chosen annotation, and inject `readOnly: true`. More code, but keeps the LinkML schema authoritative and encodes the rule once. 3. **Annotation as a signal, plus option 1 or 2.** Put `annotations: {readOnly: true}` (or `readonly: "..."`) on the slot in the LinkML schema (potentially injected via `-M`/`-O` in this project's pipeline), and have a post-processor or subclassed generator pick it up. Gives a declarative marker in the LinkML schema even though the stock generator ignores it. For a small number of slots, option 1 is the pragmatic choice. For many slots or recurring use, option 2 (driven by `readonly` or an annotation) scales better. ## Possible roles for `pydantic2linkml` To be clear about what is and is not in scope for *this* project: - `pydantic2linkml` produces LinkML, not JSON Schema. It cannot, on its own, cause `readOnly` to appear in a downstream JSON Schema — the LinkML → JSON Schema step is owned by [`linkml`][jsg]. - This project already supports `-M` (deep merge) and `-O` (overlay) against the generated LinkML, so users can already inject `readonly` values or annotations onto slots without any code change here. - Documenting the recommended pattern for producing JSON Schema `readOnly` from a Pydantic-rooted pipeline once LinkML upstream settles on a mapping. ## Asks - [x] Confirm the framing above is accurate. - [ ] Decide whether this project should wait on the upstream LinkML discussion before taking any action, or whether it should adopt one of the workaround options in the meantime so that Pydantic `json_schema_extra={"readOnly": True}` markers (as used by [`dandischema.models`][dandi-models]) round-trip through to the downstream JSON Schema. ## References - [LinkML metamodel `readonly` slot definition][lk-readonly] - [JSON Schema 2019-09 `readOnly` keyword][js-readonly] - [`linkml` `JsonSchemaGenerator` docs][jsg] - [Pydantic `Field` / `json_schema_extra`][pyd-jse] - [`dandischema.models` — example Pydantic source using `json_schema_extra={"readOnly": True}`][dandi-models] - The forthcoming `linkml/linkml` issue proposing that `JsonSchemaGenerator` emit `readOnly: true` when a slot has a non-empty `readonly` value.

title:	`JsonSchemaGenerator`: emit `readOnly: true` for slots with a `readonly` meta slot value
state:	OPEN
author:	candleindark (Isaac To)
labels:	
comments:	0
assignees:	
projects:	
milestone:	
number:	3528
--
**What is your feature request?**

Have `JsonSchemaGenerator` emit JSON Schema [`readOnly: true`][js-readonly]
for any slot whose [`readonly`][lk-readonly] meta slot has a non-empty
value.

JSON Schema's `readOnly` is well-specified: a non-validating annotation
indicating the instance value is managed by the owning authority and
should not be modified by consumers. LinkML's `readonly` is defined more
vaguely ("If present, slot is read only. Text explains why."), but its
intent is close enough that emitting `readOnly: true` is a reasonable
default mapping. Neither keyword affects validation, so the mapping is
safe. The LinkML `readonly` value is a free-text reason with no JSON
Schema equivalent; it could optionally be preserved as a custom
annotation (e.g., `x-readonly-reason`), or simply dropped 
for the JSON Schema target.

`readOnly` is part of the default JSON Schema 2019-09 meta-data
vocabulary, so no dialect change is needed.

**How important is this feature to you?**

Important — we want the LinkML schema to be the single source of
truth. The available workarounds (post-process the generated JSON
Schema, or subclass `JsonSchemaGenerator`) mean that publishing the
LinkML schema alone is not enough: anyone who needs the correct JSON
Schema also has to receive and run our post-processor, which
undermines the schema-as-source-of-truth story. With this mapping
built in, upstream-Pydantic pipelines (e.g.
`Field(..., json_schema_extra={"readOnly": True})` as used in
[`dandischema.models`][dandi-models], round-tripped through
[`pydantic2linkml`][p2l]) would preserve `readOnly` end-to-end without
any custom plumbing on the consumer side.

**Additional context**

Discussion / verification of the semantic overlap, including a
demonstration that neither keyword affects validation behavior:
dandi/pydantic2linkml#68.

If this proposal is accepted, I am happy to submit the PR.

[lk-readonly]: https://linkml.io/linkml-model/latest/docs/readonly/
[dandi-models]: https://github.com/dandi/dandischema/blob/master/dandischema/models.py

**What is your feature request?**

Have `JsonSchemaGenerator` emit JSON Schema [`readOnly: true`][js-readonly]
for any slot whose [`readonly`][lk-readonly] meta slot has a non-empty
value.

JSON Schema's `readOnly` is well-specified: a non-validating annotation
indicating the instance value is managed by the owning authority and
should not be modified by consumers. LinkML's `readonly` is defined more
vaguely ("If present, slot is read only. Text explains why."), but its
intent is close enough that emitting `readOnly: true` is a reasonable
default mapping. Neither keyword affects validation, so the mapping is
safe. The LinkML `readonly` value is a free-text reason with no JSON
Schema equivalent; it could optionally be preserved as a custom
annotation (e.g., `x-readonly-reason`), or simply dropped 
for the JSON Schema target.

`readOnly` is part of the default JSON Schema 2019-09 meta-data
vocabulary, so no dialect change is needed.

**How important is this feature to you?**

Important — we want the LinkML schema to be the single source of
truth. The available workarounds (post-process the generated JSON
Schema, or subclass `JsonSchemaGenerator`) mean that publishing the
LinkML schema alone is not enough: anyone who needs the correct JSON
Schema also has to receive and run our post-processor, which
undermines the schema-as-source-of-truth story. With this mapping
built in, upstream-Pydantic pipelines (e.g.
`Field(..., json_schema_extra={"readOnly": True})` as used in
[`dandischema.models`][dandi-models], round-tripped through
[`pydantic2linkml`][p2l]) would preserve `readOnly` end-to-end without
any custom plumbing on the consumer side.

**Additional context**

Discussion / verification of the semantic overlap, including a
demonstration that neither keyword affects validation behavior:
dandi/pydantic2linkml#68.

If this proposal is accepted, I am happy to submit the PR.

def _get_meta_schema_validator():
    """Return a cached LinkML meta-schema validator.

    The validator is initialized lazily on first call (importing

    type in the generated JSON Schema, so unknown field names are caught
    as validation errors.

    from linkml.validator.plugins import JsonschemaValidationPlugin

    meta_schema_path = str(
        resource_files("linkml_runtime.linkml_model.model.schema").joinpath("meta.yaml")
    )
    return Validator(
        meta_schema_path,

def canonicalize_schema_yml(yml: str) -> str:
    """Canonicalize a YAML string as a LinkML schema via a round-trip.

    Deserializes ``yml`` into a ``SchemaDefinition`` object,
    re-serializes it to canonical YAML, then validates the canonical
    output against the LinkML meta schema.  This serves two purposes:

    * **Canonical ordering** — the output keys follow the same order
      produced by serializing a freshly constructed ``SchemaDefinition``.
    * **Validation** — the canonical YAML is validated against the
      LinkML meta schema.  Unknown field names and wrong-type values for
      known fields are caught and re-raised as ``InvalidLinkMLSchemaError``.

    :param yml: A YAML string to canonicalize as a LinkML schema.
    :return: Canonically ordered, validated YAML string representing the
        schema.
    :raises InvalidLinkMLSchemaError: If the resulting schema does not
        conform to the LinkML meta schema (unknown field names,
        wrong-type values, etc.).
    """
    try:
        sd = yaml_loader.loads(yml, target_class=SchemaDefinition)
    except TypeError as e:
        raise InvalidLinkMLSchemaError(f"Unknown field in schema: {e}") from e

    canonical = yaml_dumper.dumps(sd)

    validator = _get_meta_schema_validator()
    report = validator.validate(yaml.safe_load(canonical), "schema_definition")
    if report.results:
        raise InvalidLinkMLSchemaError(
            "Schema validation failed: " + "; ".join(r.message for r in report.results)
        )

    return canonical

message.content: `_READONLY_TEXT` is defined as a class attribute. It seems that you can refer to it in the parametrize argument list. Is this a standard behavior of Python?

content.text:
Yes, it's standard. The class body executes as a regular block with its own namespace, similar to a function body. Names assigned earlier in the body are in that namespace and are visible to subsequent top-level expressions in the same body — including decorator expressions like `@pytest.mark.parametrize(...)`, which are evaluated at class-body time (before the method object is bound).

The gotcha is that this *only* works at the top level of the class body. Inside a method, bare `_READONLY_TEXT` would fail with `NameError` — function scopes don't see the enclosing class scope, so you'd have to write `self._READONLY_TEXT` or `TestSlotGenerator._READONLY_TEXT`. But in the decorator on the line above the method, you're still in class-body scope, so the bare name resolves.

You're right on the mechanical point — `readonly` isn't in `AnonymousSlotExpression` (I just confirmed), so `_get_ase` would drop it for subschemas regardless. Functionally, moving the `match` outside the guard produces the same output today.

That said, I'd still keep it inside, for two reasons:

Grouping them documents intent; splitting them invites a future reader to wonder why `readonly` is treated differently.
2. **Defensive against linkml-model changes.** `title` and `description` *are* in `AnonymousSlotExpression`, which is exactly why the guard exists for them. If linkml ever adds `readonly` to `AnonymousSlotExpression`, code outside the guard would silently start emitting `readonly` on union choices — and the existing `test_subschema_excludes_readonly` would fail far from the cause. Keeping it inside is one indent level that makes the regression impossible.

The cost of keeping it inside is essentially zero. So unless you see a reason I'm missing, I'd leave the placement as-is.

## CLI Usage

```bash
pydantic2linkml [OPTIONS] MODULE_NAMES...
# Example:
pydantic2linkml -o output.yml -l INFO dandischema.models
```

Options:

- `--output-file`/`-o` (path) — write output to a file instead of stdout
- `--merge-file`/`-M` (path) — deep-merge a YAML file into the generated
  schema; values from the file win on conflict; the result is validated
  against the LinkML meta schema
- `--overlay-file`/`-O` (path) — shallow-merge a YAML file into the
  generated schema; the result is validated against the LinkML meta
  schema
- `--log-level`/`-l` (default: WARNING)

## Architecture

### Core Translation Pipeline

1. **`tools.py`** — Low-level utilities for introspecting Pydantic internals
   and post-processing the generated schema YAML:
   - `get_all_modules()` — imports modules and collects them with submodules
   - `fetch_defs()` — extracts `BaseModel` subclasses and `Enum` subclasses
     from modules
   - `get_field_schema()` / `get_locally_defined_fields()` — extracts
     resolved `pydantic_core.CoreSchema` objects for fields, distinguishing
     newly defined vs. overriding fields
   - `FieldSchema` (NamedTuple) — bundles a field's core schema, its
     resolution context, field name, `FieldInfo`, owning model, and an
     `is_subschema` flag (default `False`) indicating whether this
     represents a sub-schema in the schema of a field (e.g., a union
     choice) rather than the schema of the field itself
   - `resolve_ref_schema()` — resolves `definition-ref` and `definitions`
     schema types to concrete schemas
   - `canonicalize_schema_yml(yml)` — round-trips a YAML string through
     `SchemaDefinition` for canonical key ordering, then validates the
     result against the LinkML meta schema via `linkml.validator`
     (raises `InvalidLinkMLSchemaError` on unknown fields or wrong-type
     values); the meta-schema validator is lazily initialized and cached
     via `_get_meta_schema_validator()`
   - `apply_schema_overlay(schema_yml, overlay_file)` — shallow-merges a
     YAML file into a schema YAML string; no field filtering; calls
     `canonicalize_schema_yml` to reorder keys and validate the result
   - `apply_yaml_deep_merge(schema_yml, merge_file)` — deep-merges a YAML
     file into a schema YAML string using `deepmerge`; calls
     `canonicalize_schema_yml` to reorder keys and validate the result
   - `remove_schema_key_duplication(yml)` — strips redundant `name`/`text`/
     `prefix_prefix` fields from serialized LinkML YAML
   - `add_section_breaks(yml)` — inserts blank lines before top-level
     sections

2. **`gen_linkml.py`** — Main translation logic:
   - `translate_defs(module_names)` — top-level entry point; loads modules, fetches defs, runs `LinkmlGenerator`
   - `LinkmlGenerator` — single-use class; converts a collection of Pydantic models and enums into a `SchemaDefinition`. Call `generate()` once per instance.
   - `SlotGenerator` — single-use class; translates a single Pydantic `CoreSchema` into a `SlotDefinition`. Dispatches on schema `type` strings via handler methods. Handles nesting, optionality, lists, unions, literals, UUIDs, dates, etc.

3. **`cli/`** — Typer-based CLI wrapping `translate_defs`; `cli/__init__.py`
   defines the `app` and `main` command. After translation the pipeline is:
   dump YAML → optional `-M` deep merge → optional `-O` overlay →
   `remove_schema_key_duplication` → `add_section_breaks` → output.

   - `NameCollisionError` — duplicate class/enum names across modules
   - `GeneratorReuseError` — attempting to reuse a single-use generator
   - `TranslationNotImplementedError` — schema type not yet handled
   - `SlotUsageGenerationError` — cannot generate a slot_usage entry to
     make a base slot function like a target slot. A slot_usage entry can
     extend the base slot with new properties, override the base slot's
     non-constraint properties, and apply allowed monotonic refinements
     to its constraint properties (those defined in `SlotExpression`).
     The set of allowed refinements is defined by
     `_is_allowed_constraint_refinement` in `tools.py`. Any other change
     in a constraint property, or any meta slot missing from the target

     case-insensitively on construction. The "disallowed varied" framing

     allowed monotonic refinements are emitted into the slot_usage entry
     instead.

     not a mapping)
   - `InvalidLinkMLSchemaError` — schema does not conform to the LinkML
     meta schema (unknown fields, wrong-type values, etc.); raised by
     `canonicalize_schema_yml`

### Test Assets

`tests/assets/mock_module0.py` and `mock_module1.py` define Pydantic models used across test files to exercise the translator with realistic model hierarchies.

## Test Writing Conventions

- Group related tests into a class.
- Use parametrization to reduce code duplication.
